notes.definition: Collision theory states that chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other with sufficient energy. The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react is called the activation energy.
explanation: Collision theory explains how various factors affect the rates of reactions. According to this theory, chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy. The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react is called the activation energy. A collision with less energy than this does not cause a reaction. The rate of reaction depends on the number of successful collisions per second, which depends on how often particles collide (the frequency of collisions) and how energetic the collisions are.

Increasing the concentration of reactants in solution means there are more reactant particles in the same volume. The particles collide more often, so the frequency of collisions increases and the rate increases. In the same way, increasing the pressure of reacting gases squeezes the same number of gas particles into a smaller volume (or adds more particles to the same volume), so collisions are more frequent and the rate increases.

Increasing the surface area of a solid reactant, for example by cutting it into smaller pieces or using a powder, exposes more particles at the surface. Only particles at the surface can collide with particles of the other reactant, so with a larger surface area to volume ratio there are more frequent collisions and the rate increases. The total amount of product is not changed, only how quickly it forms.

Increasing the temperature makes particles move faster. This has two effects. Faster particles collide more frequently, and they collide with more energy, so a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy. Both effects increase the number of successful collisions per second. Because of the second effect, temperature usually has a bigger effect on rate than you would expect from the increase in collision frequency alone.

You can use simple ideas about proportionality. If the concentration of a reactant is doubled, there are twice as many reactant particles in the same volume, so the frequency of collisions doubles and, for many reactions, the rate doubles. The time taken for the reaction to reach a certain point then halves. In exams, always say 'more frequent collisions' or 'more collisions per second', not just 'more collisions', because the total number of collisions is not what matters; what matters is how many happen in a given time.
keyFacts: Reactions occur only when particles collide with sufficient energy.
Activation energy is the minimum energy particles must have to react.
Rate depends on the frequency of successful collisions.
Higher concentration: more particles in the same volume, more frequent collisions.
Higher gas pressure: more particles in the same volume, more frequent collisions.
Larger surface area: more particles exposed, more frequent collisions.
Higher temperature: particles move faster, so more frequent collisions and more energetic collisions.
At higher temperature a greater proportion of collisions have at least the activation energy.
If the frequency of collisions doubles, the rate (often) doubles.

keyTerms.definition: The idea that reactions occur only when reacting particles collide with each other with sufficient energy.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react.
A collision between reacting particles with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, which leads to a reaction.
The number of collisions per second.
The surface area of a solid divided by its volume; higher for smaller pieces.
Two quantities change by the same factor; if one doubles, the other doubles.

workedExamples.title: Explaining a temperature change
workedExamples.question: Explain why magnesium reacts faster with acid at 40 °C than at 20 °C.
steps: At higher temperature the particles have more energy and move faster.
So they collide more frequently (more collisions per second).
And a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.
So there are more successful collisions per second.
workedExamples.answer: More frequent and more energetic collisions, so more successful collisions per second and a faster rate.

workedExamples.title: Using proportionality
workedExamples.question: The rate of a reaction is directly proportional to the concentration of acid. With 0.5 mol/dm³ acid the rate is 0.20 cm³/s. Predict the rate with 1.5 mol/dm³ acid.
steps: 1.5 ÷ 0.5 = 3, so the concentration is three times greater.
There are three times as many acid particles in the same volume, so collisions are three times as frequent.

workedExamples.title: Halving the concentration
workedExamples.question: A reaction takes 40 s with 2.0 mol/dm³ acid. Rate is proportional to concentration. How long will it take with 1.0 mol/dm³ acid?
steps: Halving the concentration halves the frequency of collisions, so the rate halves.
If the rate halves, the time doubles: 40 × 2 = 80 s.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write 'there are more collisions' to explain a faster rate.
misconceptions.right: In fact the key idea is more frequent collisions (more collisions per second).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think increasing concentration makes particles move faster or collide with more energy.
misconceptions.right: In fact only temperature changes the energy of collisions; concentration, pressure and surface area change only the frequency.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think every collision causes a reaction.
misconceptions.right: In fact only collisions with energy at least equal to the activation energy are successful.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think raising the temperature lowers the activation energy.
misconceptions.right: In fact the activation energy stays the same; more particles have enough energy to reach it.

realWorld: Food is kept in a fridge or freezer: at low temperature particles move more slowly, so the reactions that spoil food are slower.
Fine flour, sugar or coal dust in the air can explode because the huge surface area allows extremely frequent collisions with oxygen.
Cooking in a pressure cooker is faster because water boils at a higher temperature, increasing the rate of the cooking reactions.
Industrial gas reactions are often run at high pressure to increase the frequency of collisions.
examTips: Use the phrase 'more frequent collisions' or 'more collisions per second', never just 'more collisions'.
For temperature, give both effects: more frequent collisions and more energetic collisions (more with energy ≥ activation energy).
For concentration and pressure, say 'more particles in the same volume'.
For surface area, say 'more particles are exposed', not 'more surface particles are made'.
When explaining proportionality, say that doubling the number of particles in the same volume doubles the frequency of collisions.
summary: Reactions need collisions with energy at least equal to the activation energy.
Concentration, pressure and surface area increase the frequency of collisions.
Temperature increases both the frequency and the energy of collisions.
More successful collisions per second means a faster rate.
Doubling concentration often doubles the rate and halves the time.

questions.question: According to collision theory, what must happen for particles to react?
options: They must be in a solution
They must collide with sufficient energy
They must be the same size
markScheme: 1 mark: collide with sufficient energy
questions.explanation: Particles react only when they collide with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy. Many reactions happen without heating or outside solution.

questions.question: What is the name of the minimum amount of energy particles must have to react?
markScheme: 1 mark: activation energy
questions.explanation: Activation energy is the minimum energy needed for a collision to be successful.

questions.question: Why does increasing the concentration of an acid increase the rate of its reaction with zinc?
options: There are more acid particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent
markScheme: 1 mark: more particles in the same volume, more frequent collisions
questions.explanation: Concentration affects only how often particles collide. It does not change particle speed, collision energy or activation energy.

questions.question: What happens to the particles in a reaction mixture when the temperature is increased?
markScheme: 1 mark: they move faster
questions.explanation: At a higher temperature particles have more kinetic energy and move faster, which leads to more frequent and more energetic collisions.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction?
options: Particles collide more frequently, but with less energy
The concentration of the reactants increases
Particles collide more frequently and more of the collisions have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy
markScheme: 1 mark: more frequent collisions and more collisions with at least the activation energy
questions.explanation: Temperature has two effects: more frequent collisions and more energetic collisions. It does not change the activation energy or the concentration.

questions.question: Two gases react together. Why does increasing the pressure increase the rate of reaction?
options: The gas particles have more energy
The activation energy is lower at higher pressure
There are more gas particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent
markScheme: 1 mark: more particles in the same volume, more frequent collisions
questions.explanation: Higher pressure means the gas particles are closer together, so they collide more often. Their energy is unchanged at the same temperature.

questions.question: Why does magnesium powder react faster with acid than the same mass of magnesium ribbon?
options: Powder has a larger surface area, so more particles are exposed to collide with acid particles
Powder increases the concentration of the acid
markScheme: 1 mark: larger surface area, more particles exposed, more frequent collisions
questions.explanation: Only magnesium atoms at the surface can be hit by acid particles. Powder exposes many more, so collisions are more frequent.

questions.question: Which change increases both the frequency of collisions and the energy of collisions?
options: Increasing the pressure of a gas
markScheme: 1 mark: increasing the temperature
questions.explanation: Concentration, pressure and surface area only increase collision frequency. Only temperature also increases the energy of the collisions.

questions.question: Increasing the temperature by 10 °C increases the frequency of collisions by only a few per cent, yet the rate of reaction often doubles. Why?
options: The concentration of the reactants doubles
A much greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy
The particles become larger and easier to hit
markScheme: 1 mark: a greater proportion of collisions have at least the activation energy
questions.explanation: The main effect of temperature is that many more collisions have enough energy to react. The increase in collision frequency is small by comparison.

questions.question: A student explains why a more concentrated acid reacts faster. Which explanation would gain full credit?
options: The particles have more energy so collide harder
The particles move faster so collide more
There are more particles in the same volume, so there are more frequent collisions
markScheme: 1 mark: more particles in the same volume, more frequent collisions
questions.explanation: 'More collisions' is not enough; the rate depends on collisions per second. Concentration does not change particle energy or speed.

questions.question: The rate of a reaction is directly proportional to the concentration of acid. The concentration of acid is doubled. By what factor does the rate increase?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2 (the rate doubles)
questions.explanation: Doubling the concentration doubles the number of acid particles in the same volume, so the frequency of collisions doubles and the rate doubles.

questions.question: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 1 cm. Give your answer as the number x in the ratio x : 1.
markScheme: 1 mark: surface area = 6 × 1 × 1 = 6 cm², volume = 1 cm³
1 mark: ratio 6 : 1
questions.explanation: A 1 cm cube has six faces of 1 cm², so 6 cm² of surface for 1 cm³ of volume.

questions.question: The rate of a reaction is directly proportional to the concentration of acid. With 0.5 mol/dm³ acid the rate is 0.20 cm³/s. Predict the rate with 1.5 mol/dm³ acid.
markScheme: 1 mark: concentration is 3 times greater (1.5 ÷ 0.5 = 3)
1 mark: rate = 3 × 0.20 = 0.60 cm³/s
questions.explanation: Three times as many acid particles in the same volume gives three times the frequency of collisions, so the rate is three times greater.

questions.question: A reaction takes 40 s to finish with 2.0 mol/dm³ acid. The rate is directly proportional to the concentration. Predict how long it would take with 1.0 mol/dm³ acid.
markScheme: 1 mark: halving concentration halves the rate
1 mark: so the time doubles: 40 × 2 = 80 s
questions.explanation: Half the concentration means half as many particles in the same volume, so collisions are half as frequent. The reaction takes twice as long.

questions.question: In a gas reaction, the rate is directly proportional to the pressure. At 100 kPa the rate is 0.004 mol/s. Predict the rate at 200 kPa.
markScheme: 1 mark: pressure doubles so rate doubles: 2 × 0.004 = 0.008 mol/s
questions.explanation: Doubling the pressure doubles the number of gas particles in the same volume, so collisions are twice as frequent.

questions.question: A student finds that the rate of a reaction roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise in temperature. At 20 °C the rate is 0.05 /s. Predict the rate at 40 °C.
markScheme: 1 mark: 20 °C rise is two 10 °C steps, so the rate doubles twice (× 4)
questions.explanation: From 20 °C to 30 °C the rate doubles to 0.10 /s; from 30 °C to 40 °C it doubles again to 0.20 /s. A common mistake is to double only once.

questions.question: State the two conditions needed for reacting particles to react, according to collision theory.
markScheme: 1 mark: the particles must collide
1 mark: with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy (sufficient energy)
questions.explanation: Both are needed: a collision, and enough energy in that collision.

questions.question: Define activation energy.
acceptedAnswers: minimum energy particles must have to react
markScheme: 1 mark: the minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react
questions.explanation: The word 'minimum' is essential.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of particles, why increasing the concentration of hydrochloric acid increases the rate of its reaction with calcium carbonate.
acceptedAnswers: more acid particles in the same volume
markScheme: 1 mark: more acid particles in the same volume
1 mark: so more frequent collisions (more collisions per second)
questions.explanation: The answer must refer to frequency (per second), not just 'more collisions'.

questions.question: Explain why powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster with acid than marble chips of the same mass.
markScheme: 1 mark: powder has a larger surface area (to volume ratio) / more particles exposed
1 mark: so more frequent collisions with acid particles
questions.explanation: More exposed particles means acid particles can collide with the solid more often.

questions.question: Explain why the rate of reaction between magnesium and acid decreases as the reaction goes on.
markScheme: 1 mark: reactants are used up / the concentration of acid decreases
1 mark: so there are fewer reactant particles in the same volume and less frequent collisions
questions.explanation: As the reaction proceeds there are fewer acid particles left, so collisions become less frequent and the rate falls.

questions.question: Use collision theory to explain why food goes off more slowly in a fridge.
markScheme: 1 mark: at low temperature particles move more slowly / have less energy
1 mark: so collisions are less frequent and fewer have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so the reactions are slower
questions.explanation: The reactions that spoil food (and the microorganisms that cause them) are slowed down when particles have less energy.

questions.question: Explain fully why increasing the temperature increases the rate of a reaction.
markScheme: 1 mark: particles gain energy and move faster
1 mark: so they collide more frequently
1 mark: and more collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so there are more successful collisions per second
questions.explanation: A full answer gives both effects of temperature: collision frequency and collision energy.

questions.question: Explain why doubling the concentration of a reactant in solution can double the rate of reaction.
acceptedAnswers: twice as many particles in the same volume
twice as many successful collisions per second
markScheme: 1 mark: there are twice as many reactant particles in the same volume
1 mark: so the frequency of collisions (and successful collisions) doubles
questions.explanation: This uses simple proportionality: number of particles per unit volume ∝ frequency of collisions ∝ rate.

questions.question: A student says: 'Raising the temperature makes the reaction faster only because the particles collide more often.' Evaluate this statement.
markScheme: 1 mark: partly correct: particles do move faster and collide more frequently
1 mark: but the statement is incomplete: collisions are also more energetic, so a greater proportion have at least the activation energy (this is the more important effect)
questions.explanation: Temperature is the only factor that increases both the frequency and the energy of collisions.

questions.question: Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid. Use collision theory to explain how increasing (a) the concentration of the acid, (b) the surface area of the calcium carbonate and (c) the temperature affects the rate of this reaction.
markScheme: Indicative content: reactions occur only when particles collide with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy; rate depends on the frequency of successful collisions; (a) higher concentration: more acid particles in the same volume, so more frequent collisions, so faster rate; (b) larger surface area (smaller pieces or powder): more calcium carbonate particles exposed to the acid, so more frequent collisions, so faster rate; (c) higher temperature: particles move faster so collide more frequently; and collisions are more energetic so a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy; so more successful collisions per second, faster rate; only temperature changes the energy of collisions.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all three factors explained correctly using collision frequency, with temperature also explained in terms of energy and activation energy.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): two factors explained correctly, or all three with some imprecision (for example 'more collisions' without frequency).
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements that the factors increase the rate, with little or no explanation.
questions.explanation: Use the language of frequency: more collisions per second. Temperature is the only one of the three that also makes collisions more energetic.

questions.question: Flour is not dangerous when it is stored in sacks, but a cloud of fine flour dust in the air of a flour mill can explode if there is a spark. Use collision theory to explain this.
markScheme: Indicative content: flour reacts with oxygen (combustion); in a sack, the flour has a small surface area exposed to the air, so collisions with oxygen are infrequent and the rate is very slow; fine dust has a very large surface area to volume ratio; each tiny particle is surrounded by air, so there are very frequent collisions between flour and oxygen particles; the spark provides the activation energy for some particles; the reaction is exothermic, so the energy released gives more particles energy greater than the activation energy and raises the temperature; this increases collision frequency and energy further; the reaction becomes extremely fast and spreads through the dust, releasing gases and energy suddenly, which is an explosion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear explanation linking large surface area to very frequent collisions, the spark to activation energy, and the energy released to the speed of the reaction.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple points, for example dust has a larger surface area or the spark starts the reaction.
questions.explanation: A dust cloud has an enormous surface area in contact with oxygen. Once the spark supplies the activation energy, the exothermic reaction heats the surrounding dust and the reaction accelerates very rapidly.
